title: Conditions
subtitle: Six types: simple, future-more-vivid, future-less-vivid, present contrary-to-fact, past contrary-to-fact, general.
objectives: Identify the six types of conditional sentences.
Understand the protasis (if-clause) and apodosis (then-clause) structure.
Recognize contrary-to-fact conditions by imperfect/pluperfect subjunctive.

sections.heading: The six condition types
sections.body:
1. Simple (indicative in both clauses): sī hoc dīcis, errās. — If you say this, you err.

2. Future-more-vivid (future indicative in both): sī hoc dīcēs, errābis. — If you (will) say this, you will err.

3. Future-less-vivid (present subjunctive in both): sī hoc dīcās, errēs. — If you should say this, you would err.

4. Present contrary-to-fact (imperfect subjunctive in both): sī hoc dīcerēs, errārēs. — If you were saying this (but you are not), you would be erring.

5. Past contrary-to-fact (pluperfect subjunctive in both): sī hoc dīxissēs, errāvissēs. — If you had said this (but you did not), you would have erred.

6. General (present subjunctive in protasis, indicative in apodosis): sī quis hoc dīcat, errat. — If anyone says this, he errs.

items.prompt: Identify the type: sī Caesar adesset, vincerēmus.

items.answer: If Caesar were here (but he is not), we would be winning.
Future-more-vivid (future perfect in protasis, future in apodosis).

words.gloss: If Caesar were here, the enemies would flee.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can identify and translate all six condition types.
